message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) belong to very different branches of the mammalian tree:

| Taxonomic level | Lion | Zebra |
|-----------------|------|-------|
| Class | Mammalia | Mammalia |
| Sub‑class | Theria | Theria |
| Infraclass | Eutheria (placentals) | Eutheria |
| Super‑order | Laurasiatheria | Laurasiatheria |
| Order | Carnivora (Feliformia) | Perissodactyla |
| Family | Felidae | Equidae |

Because they diverge at the order level, their most recent common ancestor is the last common ancestor of the two orders **Carnivora** and **Perissodactyla**. That ancestor is a member of the clade **Laurasiatheria**, a group of placental mammals that split from other eutherians roughly 90–100 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous.

So, the common ancestor of a lion and a zebra is a small, likely insectivorous mammal that lived about 90–100 million years ago, the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatherian clade that gave rise to both carnivores and odd‑toed ungulates.

The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. The common ancestor of lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) would be a common ancestor in the mammalian lineage. Both are mammals, but lions are felids (family Felidae), zebras are equids (family Equidae). They diverged from a common ancestor in the order Carnivora vs Perissodactyla? Actually lions are in order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia. Zebras are in order Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates). So their common ancestor would be a more distant mammalian ancestor, perhaps a placental mammal ancestor. The last common ancestor of all placental mammals is the eutherian ancestor. But maybe they want the last common ancestor of the two species: that would be the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That would be the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both orders, which is the clade of Laurasiatheria? Actually Carnivora and Perissodactyla are both part of the clade Laurasiatheria. So the last common ancestor of lions and zebras would be the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria, which is a mammalian ancestor that lived about 90-100 million years ago. So the answer: the last common ancestor of the two species is a mammal that lived around 90-100 million years ago, likely a small, insectivorous mammal. But maybe the user expects "the last common ancestor of lions and zebras is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is a mammal that lived about 90-100 million years ago." Or "the last common ancestor of lions and zebras is the last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria." So answer accordingly.
